relations.note: Kashíri fathers Pavá with a mortal Asháninka woman.
They lived among humans and taught proper life before Pavá withdrew.
Some traditions use Oriya for the sun identified with Pavá.
Pawa gives Oriya the crown whose brilliance becomes sunlight.

relations.myth: Flying beings raise the dangerous Sun
relations.note: Kentíparo wraps Pavá in cushmas and carries him upward.
Neorónke fixes a vine to heaven, enabling Pavá’s ascent.

relations.myth: Daughters ascend and leave their clothing
relations.note: Pavá fathers daughters whose discarded clothing becomes seasonal trees and flowers.
Benevolent spirits and transformers are collectively described as Pavá’s children.

relations.myth: Return of a son of the Sun
relations.note: Divine children and returning civilizing emissaries bear this relational title.
relations.source: Brown and Fernández, War of Shadows

relations.note: Some traditions call the culture hero Pachakamáite a son of the Sun.

relations.myth: The living severed head of Inka
relations.note: Post-contact myths call Inka a son of Pavá who provides manufactured wealth.
relations.source: Brown and Fernández, War of Shadows

relations.note: This anti-colonial transformer is called a Pavá or god, not securely the Sun.
Evangelization applied Pavá terminology to the true Christian Father above older divinities.
Some Asháninka speakers used the Quechua name Inti for the sun.
